title: "7.1 Interaction Effects (AKA Moderation)"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

- Interaction effects are fundamental to much of health and social science
  - E.g., Much of sociology focuses on group differences. To name just a few:

:::: {.columns}

- Race-ethnicity
- Gender
- Social class
  - Educational attainment
  - Occupations
  - Income
- Politics
  - Party affiliation
  - Beliefs
  - Behavior
- Age
  - Cohorts
  - Life stages
  - Periods
:::

- Sexuality
- Religion
  - Affiliation
  - Beliefs
  - Behavior
- Space / geography
  - Countries
  - States
  - Cultures (and subcultures)

## Intersecting effects

- Often, we think an effect may operate differently across contexts or groups
  - Will a new medical treatment be equally effective across all ages?
  - Does aging result in declining physical health at the same rate for all racial-ethnic groups?
  - Are Democrats and Republicans similarly persuaded by a campaign ad?
  - Etc.
- Intersectionality makes this argument explicit ([Hill Collins and Bilge 2020](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Intersectionality%2C+2nd+Edition-p-9781509539673))
  - E.g., The experience of being a black woman ≠ black + woman
    - The intersection produces a unique experience and effect\*

\*See some recent empirical evidence on this in [Heiserman 2023](https://doi.org/10.1086/728051) and [Mize 2025](/research/mize_2025_spq.qmd)

## Interaction effects in linear regression

*"Interaction effects exist when the effect of one independent variable is contingent on the level of another independent variable." ([Mize 2019 p.81](https://www.sociologicalscience.com/articles-v6-4-81/))*

- In a linear regression model with no nonlinearities, consider what an interaction (product) term allows in the predictions (here with one continuous IV and one binary IV)

$$\widehat{y} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{c}c_{i} + \beta_{b}b_{i} + \beta_{cXb}{cXb}_{i} + \ldots$$

$$\widehat{{wages}_{i}} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{age}{age}_{i} + \beta_{woman}{woman}_{i} + \beta_{ageXwoman}{ageXwoman}_{i} + \ldots$$

$$\widehat{{wages}_{i}} = 4.09 + 0.26{age}_{i} + 0.00{woman}_{i} - 0.13{ageXwoman}_{i} + \ldots$$

- What does the coefficient on the interaction (product) term represent?
  - Do men and women receive the same returns for aging?

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss", clear

*7.1.a & 7.1.b - linear model interaction ex: continuous X binary
qui regress wages i.woman c.age i.college i.race3 i.married i.parent ///
    if employed == 1
qui margins, at(age=(18(5)83) woman=(0 1))
marginsplot, noci ytitle("Predicted Hourly Wages") xtitle("Age in Years") ///
    title("[7.1.a] Predicted Hourly Wages Based on Age and Gender", size(medium)) ///
    subtitle("Intercept Shift - No Interaction Term") ylabel(0(5)30) ///
    xlabel(20(10)80) legend(position(6)) saving(noint, replace)

qui regress wages i.woman##c.age i.college i.race3 i.married i.parent ///
    if employed == 1
qui margins, at(age=(18(5)83) woman=(0 1))
marginsplot, noci ytitle("Predicted Hourly Wages") xtitle("Age in Years") ///
    title("[7.1.b] Predicted Hourly Wages Based on Age and Gender", size(medium)) ///
    subtitle("Interaction Term: Age X Gender") ylabel(0(5)30) ///
    xlabel(20(10)80) legend(position(6)) saving(intterm, replace)

graph combine noint.gph intterm.gph
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-07_01_a_b-interaction.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-07_01_a_b-interaction.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.1.a and 7.1.b] Two panels of predicted hourly wages by age (18 to 83) for men and women. Left, with no interaction term: two parallel rising lines, men above women by the same amount at every age. Right, with an age by gender interaction term: men's line rises more steeply than women's, so the gender gap widens with age."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.1.a and 7.1.b] Two panels of predicted hourly wages by age (18 to 83) for men and women. Left, with no interaction term: two parallel rising lines, men above women by the same amount at every age. Right, with an age by gender interaction term: men's line rises more steeply than women's, so the gender gap widens with age."
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(dplyr)           # data manipulation
library(ggplot2)         # graphs
library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects
library(cleanplots)      # graph scheme
cleanplots_defaults()

gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta")

# Keep model variables for the employed; drop any missing data
emp <- gss |>
  filter(employed == 1) |>
  select(wages, woman, age, college, race3, married, parent)
emp <- emp[complete.cases(emp), ] |>
  mutate(across(c(woman, college, race3, married, parent), as_factor))

# 7.1.a & 7.1.b - linear model interaction ex: continuous X binary
noint <- lm(wages ~ woman + age + college + race3 + married + parent, data = emp)
intterm <- lm(wages ~ woman * age + college + race3 + married + parent, data = emp)

grid <- datagrid(model = noint, age = seq(18, 83, 5), woman = unique,
  grid_type = "counterfactual")
pr <- bind_rows(
  "[7.1.a] Intercept Shift - No Interaction Term" =
    avg_predictions(noint, by = c("age", "woman"), newdata = grid),
  "[7.1.b] Interaction Term: Age X Gender" =
    avg_predictions(intterm, by = c("age", "woman"), newdata = grid),
  .id = "model")

ggplot(pr, aes(x = age, y = estimate, color = woman)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ model, labeller = label_wrap_gen(35)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(20, 80, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, 5), limits = c(0, 30)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted Hourly Wages Based on Age and Gender",
    x = "Age in Years", y = "Predicted Hourly Wages", color = NULL)
```

:::

## Ex interaction effect with nominal IVs

- What about when we have only nominal IVs in the interaction?
  - Consider what an interaction (product) term allows in the predictions (using two binary IVs for simplicity)

$$\widehat{y} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{b1}{b1}_{i} + \beta_{b2}{b2}_{i} + \beta_{b1Xb2}{b1Xb2}_{i} + \ldots$$

$$\widehat{{wages}_{i}} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{woman}{woman}_{i} + \beta_{college}{college}_{i} + \beta_{womanXcollege}{womanXcollege}_{i} + \ldots$$

$$\widehat{{wages}_{i}} = 6.36 - 4.72{woman}_{i} + 10.47{college}_{i} - 1.56{womanXcollege}_{i} + \ldots$$

- What does the coefficient on the interaction (product) term represent?
  - Is college the great equalizer? Does it reduce the gender gap?

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*7.1.c & 7.1.d - linear model interaction ex: binary X binary
qui regress wages i.woman i.college c.age i.race4 i.married i.parent
est store no_int

qui margins college, at(woman=0) post
est store pr_men

est restore no_int
qui margins college, at(woman=1) post
est store pr_wom

coefplot pr_men pr_wom, ///
    recast(bar) vertical barw(0.3) citop ///
    ylab(0(5)35) legend(order(1 "Men" 3 "Women") pos(6) row(1)) ///
    ytitle("Hourly wages") ///
    xtitle("Educational attainment") ///
    title("[7.1.c] Hourly wages by gender and education") ///
    subtitle("No interaction term") saving(bin_no, replace)

*add an interaction
qui regress wages i.woman##i.college c.age i.race4 i.married i.parent
est store w_int

qui margins college, at(woman=0) post
est store pr_men

est restore w_int
qui margins college, at(woman=1) post
est store pr_wom

coefplot pr_men pr_wom, ///
    recast(bar) vertical barw(0.3) citop ///
    ylab(0(5)35) legend(order(1 "Men" 3 "Women") pos(6) row(1)) ///
    ytitle("Hourly wages") ///
    xtitle("Educational attainment") ///
    title("[7.1.d] Hourly wages by gender and education") ///
    subtitle("Including gender X college interaction") saving(bin_int, replace)

graph combine bin_no.gph bin_int.gph
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-07_01_c_d-interaction.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-07_01_c_d-interaction.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.1.c and 7.1.d] Two bar charts of predicted hourly wages by college degree for men and women. Left, with no interaction term: about $16 for men and $11 for women without a degree, and about $26 for men and $21 for women with a degree, the same gap at both levels. Right, with a gender by college interaction: about $16 and $11 without a degree, and about $26.5 and $20 with a degree, a wider gender gap among college graduates."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.1.c and 7.1.d] Two bar charts of predicted hourly wages by college degree for men and women. Left, with no interaction term: about $16 for men and $11 for women without a degree, and about $26 for men and $21 for women with a degree, the same gap at both levels. Right, with a gender by college interaction: about $16 and $11 without a degree, and about $26.5 and $20 with a degree, a wider gender gap among college graduates."
# Keep model variables; drop any missing data
wg <- gss |>
  select(wages, woman, college, age, race4, married, parent)
wg <- wg[complete.cases(wg), ] |>
  mutate(across(c(woman, college, race4, married, parent), as_factor))

# 7.1.c & 7.1.d - linear model interaction ex: binary X binary
no_int <- lm(wages ~ woman + college + age + race4 + married + parent, data = wg)
w_int <- lm(wages ~ woman * college + age + race4 + married + parent, data = wg)

grid <- datagrid(model = no_int, college = unique, woman = unique,
  grid_type = "counterfactual")
pr <- bind_rows(
  "[7.1.c] No interaction term" =
    avg_predictions(no_int, by = c("college", "woman"), newdata = grid),
  "[7.1.d] Including gender X college interaction" =
    avg_predictions(w_int, by = c("college", "woman"), newdata = grid),
  .id = "model")

ggplot(pr, aes(x = college, y = estimate, fill = woman)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(.7), width = .6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
    position = position_dodge(.7), width = .1) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, labeller = label_wrap_gen(35)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 35, 5), limits = c(0, 35)) +
  labs(title = "Hourly wages by gender and education",
    x = "Educational attainment", y = "Hourly wages", fill = NULL)
```

:::

\*For details on gender inequality for highly educated workers see [Quadlin et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssresearch.2023.102873)

## Nonlinear interaction effects

- For any nonlinear model, the coefficient on the interaction term is not a test of interaction (e.g., logit and probit). Why?
- Consider the variation in possible relationships *observed in your data* from a single parameter estimate (β = 0.05 for a continuous IV)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// Exs of possible effects in predictions given same beta //
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/scireview3", clear

*7.1.e - full logit curve; OR = 1.05
qui logit faculty i.fellow c.totpub c.phd

qui margins, at(totpub=(-120(10)120))
marginsplot, noci ylabel(0(0.2)1) xlabel(-120(20)120) ///
    xtitle("X") ytitle("Pr(Y)") title("[7.1.e] Beta = 0.05 ; OR =  1.05")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-07_01_e-interaction_logit.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-07_01_e-interaction_logit.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.1.e] The full S-shaped logit curve of Pr(Y) for X from -120 to 120 with beta = 0.05: near 0 below X = -60, rising steeply through about 0.4 at X = 0, and leveling off near 1 above X = 60."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.1.e] The full S-shaped logit curve of Pr(Y) for X from -120 to 120 with beta = 0.05: near 0 below X = -60, rising steeply through about 0.4 at X = 0, and leveling off near 1 above X = 60."
# Exs of possible effects in predictions given same beta
sci <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/scireview3.dta") |>
  mutate(fellow = as_factor(fellow))

# 7.1.e - full logit curve; OR = 1.05
scimod <- glm(faculty ~ fellow + totpub + phd, data = sci,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

pr_x <- function(xvals) {
  avg_predictions(scimod, by = "totpub",
    newdata = datagrid(totpub = xvals, grid_type = "counterfactual"))
}

ggplot(pr_x(seq(-120, 120, 10)), aes(x = totpub, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(color = "red") +
  geom_point(color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-120, 120, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, .2), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "[7.1.e] Beta = 0.05 ; OR =  1.05", x = "X", y = "Pr(Y)")
```

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
qui margins, at(totpub=(-120(5)-20))
marginsplot, noci ylabel(0(0.2)1) xlabel(-120(20)-20) xtitle("X")  ///
    ytitle("Pr(Y)") title("Beta = 0.05 ; OR =  1.05") name(ex1, replace)

qui margins, at(totpub=(-60(10)60))
marginsplot, noci ylabel(0(0.2)1) xlabel(-60(20)60) xtitle("X") ///
    ytitle("Pr(Y)") title("Beta = 0.05 ; OR =  1.05") name(ex2, replace)

qui margins, at(totpub=(-20(2.5)20))
marginsplot, noci ylabel(0(0.2)1) xlabel(-20(10)20) xtitle("X") ///
    ytitle("Pr(Y)") title("Beta = 0.05 ; OR =  1.05") name(ex3, replace)

qui margins, at(totpub=(40(5)120))
marginsplot, noci ylabel(0(0.2)1) xlabel(40(10)120) xtitle("X") ///
    ytitle("Pr(Y)") title("Beta = 0.05 ; OR =  1.05") name(ex4, replace)

*7.1.f
graph combine ex1 ex2 ex3 ex4, ///
    title("[7.1.f] Different effects on probs. despite identical OR = 1.05")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>

<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-07_01_f-interaction_logit.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.1.f] Four panels showing parts of the same logit curve (beta = 0.05) over different ranges of X: from -120 to -20 the probability barely rises from 0 to about 0.2; from -60 to 60 it rises steeply in an S shape from about 0.03 to 0.93; from -20 to 20 it rises almost linearly from about 0.2 to 0.65; from 40 to 120 it is nearly flat, from about 0.84 to 1."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.1.f] Four panels showing parts of the same logit curve (beta = 0.05) over different ranges of X: from -120 to -20 the probability barely rises from 0 to about 0.2; from -60 to 60 it rises steeply in an S shape from about 0.03 to 0.93; from -20 to 20 it rises almost linearly from about 0.2 to 0.65; from 40 to 120 it is nearly flat, from about 0.84 to 1."
# 7.1.f - the same curve over four ranges of X
pr4 <- bind_rows(
  "X from -120 to -20" = pr_x(seq(-120, -20, 5)),
  "X from -60 to 60" = pr_x(seq(-60, 60, 10)),
  "X from -20 to 20" = pr_x(seq(-20, 20, 2.5)),
  "X from 40 to 120" = pr_x(seq(40, 120, 5)),
  .id = "range") |>
  mutate(range = factor(range, levels = unique(range)))

ggplot(pr4, aes(x = totpub, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(color = "red") +
  geom_point(color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ range, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, .2), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "[7.1.f] Different effects on probs. despite identical OR = 1.05",
    x = "X", y = "Pr(Y)")
```

:::

### Inherently interactive nature of logit/probit models

![](images/berry-2010-logit.png){width=55% fig-alt="Panel A from Berry, DeMeritt, and Esarey (2010), an illustrative logit model without a product term: three S-shaped curves of Pr(Y) against X1 for X2 = 0, 1, and 2, shifted left as X2 increases. The marginal effect of X1 at X1 = 6 is .105 on one curve but only .018 on another."}

Figure from [Berry, DeMeritt, and Esarey 2010 *AJPS*](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2009.00429.x)

- In the example above with one continuous IV and one nominal IV, the logit/probit model is interactive because of intercept shifts produced by the nominal IV
  - That is, **the β coefficient (which determines the slope) is invariant** across the levels of the nominal IV
  - **The effect on the probabilities is not constant** due to the intercept shift
    - This is because of **"compression"**---i.e. that the predicted probability curve flattens at Pr(y) = 0 and Pr(y) = 1---thus all three of the curves above converge/compress to have the same slope at both extremes
- Consider the following example with real data (Add Health Wave 4)
  - Pr(Employed) for mothers and fathers, based on years of education completed

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// Logit Examples w/ and w/o interaction terms //
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/addhealth4", clear

*Intercept Shift in Logit
qui logit employed c.edyrs i.woman if parrole == 1, or nolog
est store intshift

*7.1.g - Estimate MEs at various places in data
mtable, dydx(edyrs) at(woman=(0 1) edyrs=(0 10 20 25))

qui margins, at(edyrs=(0(1)25) woman=(0 1))
marginsplot, noci legend(order(1 "Fathers" 2 "Mothers")) ///
    ytitle("Pr(Employed)") xtitle("Years of Education Completed") ///
    title("[7.1.g] Probability of Being Employed Based on Years of Education Completed", size(medium)) ///
    subtitle("Intercept Shift - No Interaction Term") ylabel(0(0.2)1.1) xlabel(0(5)25) ///
    text(.32 1.5 "ME = .024" .81 1.5 "ME = .022" ///
        .53 10 "ME = .024" .92 10 "ME = .012" ///
        .74 21 "ME = .015" 1.02 21 "ME = .005", size(small))
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-07_01_g-interaction_logit.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-07_01_g-interaction_logit.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.1.g] Predicted probability of being employed by years of education (0 to 25) for fathers and mothers, from a logit model with no interaction term. Fathers' probability rises from about 0.69 to 0.96 and mothers' from about 0.38 to 0.89. The marginal effect of education is about .022 for fathers and .024 for mothers at 0 years, .012 and .024 at 10 years, and .005 and .015 at 20 to 25 years: the curves converge as both approach 1."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.1.g] Predicted probability of being employed by years of education (0 to 25) for fathers and mothers, from a logit model with no interaction term. Fathers' probability rises from about 0.69 to 0.96 and mothers' from about 0.38 to 0.89. The marginal effect of education is about .022 for fathers and .024 for mothers at 0 years, .012 and .024 at 10 years, and .005 and .015 at 20 to 25 years: the curves converge as both approach 1."
# Logit Examples w/ and w/o interaction terms
ah4 <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/addhealth4.dta") |>
  filter(parrole == 1) |>
  mutate(woman = factor(woman, levels = 0:1, labels = c("Fathers", "Mothers")))

# Intercept Shift in Logit
intshift <- glm(employed ~ edyrs + woman, data = ah4,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

# 7.1.g - Estimate MEs at various places in data
slopes(intshift, variables = "edyrs",
  newdata = datagrid(woman = unique, edyrs = c(0, 10, 20, 25)))

pr_ed <- function(model, xvals) {
  avg_predictions(model, by = c("edyrs", "woman"),
    newdata = datagrid(edyrs = xvals, woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"))
}

ggplot(pr_ed(intshift, 0:25), aes(x = edyrs, y = estimate, color = woman)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  annotate("text", size = 3,
    x = c(1.5, 1.5, 10, 10, 21, 21), y = c(.32, .81, .53, .92, .74, 1.02),
    label = c("ME = .024", "ME = .022", "ME = .024", "ME = .012", "ME = .015",
      "ME = .005")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 25, 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, .2), limits = c(0, 1.1)) +
  labs(title = "[7.1.g] Probability of Being Employed Based on Years of Education Completed",
    subtitle = "Intercept Shift - No Interaction Term",
    x = "Years of Education Completed", y = "Pr(Employed)", color = NULL)
```

:::

\*Even though this is just part of the full logit curve, we still see interactive effects

#### Inherently interactive nature of logit/probit models

The full logit curve makes it easier to see that the overall slopes of the two curves are the same---the effects vary only because of the intercept shift

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## The effect of interaction terms in logit/probit

Consider the effect on the full logit curve of including an interaction (product) term

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*Add interaction/product term in logit
qui logit employed c.edyrs##i.woman if parrole == 1, or nolog
est store interact

*7.1.i - Full logit curve
qui margins, at(edyrs=(-40(2)40) woman=(0 1))
marginsplot, noci legend(order(1 "Fathers" 2 "Mothers")) ///
    ytitle("Pr(Employed)") xtitle("Years of Education Completed") ///
    title("[7.1.i] Probability of Being Employed Based on Years of Education Completed", size(medium)) ///
    subtitle("Education X Gender Interaction Term Included") ///
    ylabel(0(0.2)1) xlabel(-40(10)40)
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-07_01_i-interaction_logit.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

## Is the interaction (product) term necessary?

- There has been an intense debate in the methodological literature as to whether it is appropriate to discuss interaction effects absent an interaction (product) term in the model
- The takeaway from this research is: if you want to test for interaction, you should include the product term in the model\*
  - Not including the product term can lead to Type I (false positives) or Type II errors (false negatives). See [Rainey 2016](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-science-research-and-methods/article/compression-and-conditional-effects-a-product-term-is-essential-when-using-logistic-regression-to-test-for-interaction/98664E6FF9AA240CCDBCFFC4B29EA7F8)
- For more details, see [Appendix A7.1](appendix-a7-stata.qmd#a7.1-is-the-interaction-product-term-necessary) and/or [Mize 2019](https://www.sociologicalscience.com/articles-v6-4-81/)

\*If you test for interaction and find none, I see no issue with dropping the product term from subsequent models if you are not testing for interaction in them

## Difference in log odds ≠ difference in probs.

- Remember the coefficients summarize effects in log odds
  - For a binary IV, this is simply the (conditional) difference between the two groups
  - Differences in the probabilities (observed proportions) can be quite different than differences in the log odds

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.1.m] Two panels showing the same +.10 change in probability at three places (.05 to .15, .45 to .55, and .85 to .95). Left, on the odds curve: the odds change by +0.12, +0.40, and +13.33. Right, on the log-odds curve: the log-odds change by +1.21, +0.40, and +1.21."
# 7.1.m & 7.1.n - Log odds diff =/= diff in probabilities
# 7.1.m: three equal +.10 changes in probability, shown as odds and log-odds
pp <- data.frame(p0 = c(.05, .45, .85), p1 = c(.15, .55, .95))

podds <- "How odds change for + 0.10 increase in probability"
plo <- "How log-odds change for a + 0.10 increase in probability"
curves <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(panel = podds, p = seq(0, .95, .005)) |> mutate(y = p / (1 - p)),
  data.frame(panel = plo, p = seq(.01, .99, .005)) |> mutate(y = qlogis(p)))
steps <- bind_rows(
  pp |> mutate(panel = podds, y0 = p0 / (1 - p0), y1 = p1 / (1 - p1)),
  pp |> mutate(panel = plo, y0 = qlogis(p0), y1 = qlogis(p1))) |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("+%4.2f", y1 - y0))
curves$panel <- factor(curves$panel, levels = c(podds, plo))
steps$panel <- factor(steps$panel, levels = c(podds, plo))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(x = p, y = y), color = "red") +
  geom_segment(data = steps, aes(x = p0, xend = p1, y = y0, yend = y0),
    color = "steelblue", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(data = steps, aes(x = p1, xend = p1, y = y0, yend = y1),
    color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = steps, aes(x = p0, y = y0), color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(data = steps, aes(x = p1, y = y1), color = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(data = steps, aes(x = p1, y = y1, label = label), color = "steelblue",
    hjust = 1.1, vjust = -.4, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_wrap_gen(35)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, .2)) +
  labs(title = "[7.1.m] Change in log odds / odds does not equal change in probability",
    caption = "Each blue triangle is the same +.10 change in probability.",
    x = "Probability", y = "Odds (left) and log-odds (right)")
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.1.n] Four bar charts for groups A and B with and without evidence. Top row: log-odds of -1.50 and 1.00 for group A and 0.50 and 3.00 for group B, the same +2.5 change for both groups (no interaction in log-odds), but the probabilities are 0.18 and 0.73 for A and 0.62 and 0.95 for B, changes of .55 and .33 (an interaction in probability). # 7.1.n: bar charts for a binary x binary interaction, in log-odds and probability
# Scenario 1: same effect of evidence in log-odds (+2.5) for both groups
# Scenario 2: same effect of evidence in probability (+.40) for both groups
s1_lo <- c(-1.5, 1.0, 0.5, 3.0)
s2_p <- c(.20, .60, .55, .95)
panels <- c("No interaction in log-odds", "...but an interaction in probability",
  "An interaction in log-odds", "...but no interaction in probability")
bars <- data.frame(
  panel = rep(panels, each = 4),
  group = rep(rep(c("Group A", "Group B"), each = 2), 4),
  evidence = rep(c("No evidence", "Evidence"), 8),
  value = c(s1_lo, plogis(s1_lo), qlogis(s2_p), s2_p)) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = panels),
    evidence = factor(evidence, levels = c("No evidence", "Evidence")))

ggplot(bars, aes(x = evidence, y = value, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(.7), width = .6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%3.2f", value), vjust = ifelse(value < 0, 1.4, -.4)),
    position = position_dodge(.7), size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = .15)) +
  labs(title = "[7.1.n] Interactions can exist in log odds but not probs. (and vice versa)",
    x = NULL, y = "Log-odds (left) and probability (right)", fill = NULL)
```

:::

- Given log odds/odds are in a different metric than the probabilities, which should you trust?
  - You didn't measure or observe log odds!
  - The natural, observed "natural" metric of the data is proportions, which the probabilities model directly ([Mize 2019](https://www.sociologicalscience.com/articles-v6-4-81/))
- Methodological guidance across sociology ([Mize 2019](https://www.sociologicalscience.com/articles-v6-4-81/)), political science ([Berry et al. 2010](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2009.00429.x)), economics ([Ai and Norton 2003](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(03)00032-6)), psychology ([McCabe et al. 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2020.1868966)), and medicine ([Shiroshita et al. 2022](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192215262)) is unanimous in recommending interaction be tested in the predicted probabilities
